claims.text: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi solutionized at approximately 1100°C will have a homogeneous single-phase FCC structure.
The solutionized CoCrFeMnNi baseline contains minimal or no nanoscale precipitates.
Aging equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi at 500–650°C for 2–24 hours can induce finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
The aging treatment will produce a uniform dispersion of coherent precipitates in the FCC CoCrFeMnNi matrix.
Nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase yield strength.
Dislocations can shear coherent L12 nanoscale precipitates while retaining substantial plasticity.
Coherent or semi-coherent precipitate interfaces promote interfacial stress accommodation.
The precipitates will increase Young’s modulus or stiffness.
The nanoscale precipitates will act as barriers to crack propagation without causing severe strain localization.
The precipitates will deflect propagating cracks and improve fracture resistance.
Precipitation strengthening in FCC high- or medium-entropy alloys can improve strength without an excessive loss of ductility.
Aged equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi will exhibit a 10–20% increase in yield strength relative to the solutionized baseline.
Aged equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi will exhibit a 10–20% increase in Young’s modulus relative to the solutionized baseline.
Aging will preserve or modestly improve the ductility of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Aging will preserve or modestly improve the fracture toughness of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Excessive aging can cause precipitate coarsening and embrittlement.
The approach may fail in HEAs with unsuitable phase stability or dominant uncontrolled intermetallic formation.
Failure to achieve at least a 10% increase in both yield strength and Young’s modulus, or occurrence of substantial embrittlement, is designated as the falsification criterion.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis asserts enhanced fracture resistance, whereas the predicted outcome allows fracture toughness merely to be preserved.

The predicted-outcome field says a drop in ductility would decisively refute the hypothesis, while the formal rule requires a significant reduction in ductility and fracture toughness, leaving both the magnitude and whether both losses are required inconsistent.
